newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Ringgit sinks two pct as speculators swoop.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ringgit sinks two pct as speculators swoop.

text.p: Malaysia's ringgit sank almost two percent against the dollar on Monday as speculative selling found a fresh target and the central bank provided surprisingly little resistance, dealers and analysts said.

The ringgit hit a low of 2.5500/10 to a dollar, its weakest level since February 29, 1996. By 1032 GMT, the ringgit had improved slightly and was trading at 2.5380/10 after closing on Friday at 2.5042/52.

Dealers said Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, was believed to have provided token resistance, selling dollars at around 2.5500. Bank Negara officials were not available for comment. It usually does not comment on its open market operations.
The absence of Bank Negara in the market raised eyebrows after its governor, Ahmad Mohamed Don, last week warned of tough steps to curb speculation in the ringgit.
He said Malaysia would use all means possible to defend its currency.
Analysts had said that speculators would target the ringgit next after forcing two central banks in the region -- Thailand and the Philippines -- to effectively devalue their currencies.

"On the surface, this looks like a victory for speculators as Bank Negara is seen giving up its effort to defend the ringgit," said Sani Hamid, market analyst at research house MMS International. "However, we would not go as far as calling it a de facto devaluation."
He added it would be a big mistake to believe the central bank had given up on the ringgit.

"In fact, by staying on the sidelines, Bank Negara may have decided to wage a psychological war against speculators as it was not expected to give up after such a brief battle," Sani said. He added that by not playing to speculators' expectations, the central bank had added a touch of uncertainty to the market.
Analysts said the central bank could be waiting to hit speculators at an appropriate time.

They said Bank Negara may have realised that defending the ringgit to prove a point with speculators, and with its limited foreign exchange reserves, would be suicidal. Moreover, continued selling in dollar/ringgit would only push interest rates and swaps higher, helping those long on the swaps to make money, they added.
The central bank spent more than $1 billion last week in defence of the ringgit. At the end of June its reserves stood at 70.71 billion ringgit ($28 billion).

Analysts said the move by Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, the Philippine central bank, to allow the peso to trade in a wider range against the dollar on Friday, a de facto devaluation, had exerted greater pressures on the ringgit as well as Indonesia's rupiah.
Indonesia's central bank on Friday widened the dollar-rupiah band to 12 percent from eight percent following the Philippines' move.
The analysts said Bank Negara may be allowing market forces to dictate the spot's value rather than defend the ringgit aggressively "for a lost cause".

"It may make more sense for the central bank to let the market have its head and actually trust in the fundamental underpinnings of the economy to make sure that this forex selldown is short-lived," said Jimmy Koh, an economist at research house I.D.E.A.

"The underlying macro picture would actually allow the ringgit to bounce (back) stronger once the present feeding frenzy is over, an option seemingly not open to the likes of the Philippine peso and Thai baht," he said.
